The head is not visible, so labial pits and head scalation cannot be assessed, and Simalia, Leiopython and Corallus all include blotched arboreal forms that cannot be fully excluded. Within Morelia spilota, the pattern suggests the Coastal Carpet Python (M. s. mcdowelli) or a rainforest variant, but subspecies assignment depends largely on locality and cannot be resolved here.

This combination is characteristic of the White-lipped Python complex. Leiopython has been split into several species (including L. hoserae, L. fredparkeri, L. huonensis, L. bennettorum and L. meridionalis), and these cannot be separated from this photograph without locality or detailed scale data, so the species assignment rests on the traditional name and remains uncertain.

Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia, T. s. parietalis and T. s. fitchi can show similar red and black markings, and the subspecies assignment rests on the barred red flank pattern and the less uniformly red head than in tetrataenia, since locality is not available to confirm it.

This combination is diagnostic of the Rhinoceros Viper (Bitis nasicornis), and the pale-edged dark triangle on the crown and the lateral facial streaks agree with that identification. Bitis gabonica and B. rhinoceros have similar patterns but differ in snout structure, and the paired, stacked nasal horns visible here favour B. nasicornis.

Other members of the genus, such as Tropidolaemus subannulatus and T. philippensis, have been split from T. wagleri and can look similar, so the species assignment rests on the strongly contrasting black and yellow banding and the Sundaland form I associate with the name, but locality is needed to confirm it.

The yellow ground colour and the pattern favour the Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus) over the Green Anaconda (Eunectes murinus), which is typically olive-green with rounder, more widely spaced black spots, though the lighting and the partial view of the body leave some doubt, and Eunectes beniensis and E. deschauenseei cannot be fully excluded without locality.

Other West Indian Chilabothrus, such as C. gracilis, C. fordii and C. chrysogaster, cannot be fully excluded, and the subspecies of C. striatus (such as C. s. striatus and C. s. exagistus) depend largely on locality, which cannot be resolved here.

The yellow-brown ground colour with a dark centre or margin on most dorsal scales, producing a speckled effect, together with the dark throat band, fits the lighter savanna-edge form of the brown forest cobra, formerly treated within _N. melanoleuca_.
